q: Why is "elicitation" a better word than "gathering" for obtaining requirements?
options: Stakeholders often cannot express their needs clearly, so the information has to be drawn out
explanation: Collecting or gathering implies stakeholders already have product information ready to hand over. They often have wants, needs and ideas but cannot express them clearly, so the information is drawn out through back-and-forth interaction.
ref: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Key Concepts for Elicitation

links.label: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Key Concepts for Elicitation

q: What is the correct order of the four elicitation processes?
options: Determine approach, prepare, conduct, confirm results
Prepare, determine approach, confirm results, conduct
Conduct, confirm results, prepare, determine approach
Confirm results, conduct, determine approach, prepare
explanation: The elicitation knowledge area contains Determine Elicitation Approach, Prepare for Elicitation, Conduct Elicitation and Confirm Elicitation Results.
ref: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Table 1-2

links.label: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Table 1-2

q: How do elicitation and analysis relate?
options: All elicitation is finished and signed off before any analysis is allowed to start
Analysis replaces elicitation on agile projects
They are done by different organizations
They alternate: analysis raises new questions that need more elicitation
explanation: Elicitation is performed iteratively with analysis to progressively elaborate information. When results are vague, more questions are asked and more elicitation is done, until analysis produces no further questions or the remaining risk is acceptable.
ref: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Key Concepts for Elicitation

links.label: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Key Concepts for Elicitation

q: What does the elicitation approach describe?
options: What information to elicit, where to find it, how to obtain it and when
The test cases for the solution
explanation: The elicitation approach describes how elicitation will be performed, what information to elicit, where to find it, how to obtain it and when to conduct the activities. It may be documented or be a thought process.

q: A project manager wants to halve the elicitation effort to save time. What is the main consequence to point out?
options: The stakeholder register must be completely rewritten
Greater risk of rework and product defects later
None; elicitation can always be cut safely
explanation: Elicitation is sometimes scaled back because of constraints, but doing so introduces portfolio, program, project and product risks that may result in rework or defects. Early agreement on the appropriate amount reduces these risks.

q: An analyst has a workshop with eight stakeholders next week and starts to prepare. What should she do first?
explanation: Preparation starts with setting an objective for the activity: the reason it is being undertaken. Participants, resources, questions, the agenda and the schedule follow from it.

q: What are the three stages of any elicitation activity?
explanation: Regardless of the technique, an elicitation activity has an introduction that sets the stage and purpose, a body where questions are asked and answered, and a close that ends the activity gracefully. Follow-up then confirms the results.

q: "Describe what happens when an order arrives late." What kind of question is this?
explanation: An open-ended question allows the respondent to answer in any way they wish. A closed-ended question calls for a response from a limited list of choices.
ref: Business Analysis for Practitioners, How to Elicit Solution Information

links.label: Business Analysis for Practitioners, How to Elicit Solution Information

q: Three departments disagree about what a new system must do. Which technique is most suitable?
explanation: Facilitated workshops bring cross-functional stakeholders together and are a primary technique for quickly defining product information across domains and reconciling stakeholder differences.

q: Warehouse staff find it hard to explain the exact steps they follow when packing. Which technique should the analyst use?
explanation: Observation gives a direct view of how a process is performed. It is especially helpful for detailed processes, because stakeholders may have difficulty recalling specifics or may be unaware of their own actions.

q: An analyst sits beside call-centre agents for a day to see how they handle refunds. The agents know she is watching. What is the main drawback she should keep in mind?
options: People may act differently when they are being observed
It cannot be used at all for detailed or repetitive processes
explanation: The main drawback of the observation technique is that people may act differently when they are being observed.

q: The analyst needs input from 4,000 customers in several countries, at low cost. Which technique fits?
explanation: Questionnaires and surveys accumulate information quickly from a large number of respondents who may be widely dispersed, at relatively small cost. The typical concern is getting a sufficient response rate.

q: Users say they cannot judge the requirements until they "see something". Which technique helps?
explanation: Prototyping obtains early feedback by providing a model of the expected solution before building it. Because prototypes are tangible, stakeholders can visualize and experiment instead of discussing abstract requirements.

q: Stakeholders want to agree where the fields and buttons sit on the sign-up screen before anything is built. The analyst draws a static blueprint of that one screen. Which prototype is it?
explanation: A wireframe is a diagram representing a static blueprint or schematic of a user interface. A storyboard shows sequence or navigation through a series of images. An evolutionary prototype is the actual solution in progress.

q: Which statement about document analysis is correct?
options: It is a good way to gain background before meeting stakeholders, but documents may be out of date
It replaces the need to talk to stakeholders
It can only be used after requirements are approved
explanation: Document analysis helps the analyst understand the business environment before engaging stakeholders and can save their time. The accuracy and relevance of the information must be checked, because documentation may describe constraints that no longer apply.

q: What distinguishes a focus group?
options: It is a written set of questions
It brings together prequalified stakeholders and experts to learn their expectations and attitudes about a proposed solution
explanation: Focus groups bring together prequalified stakeholders and subject matter experts to learn about their expectations and attitudes toward a proposed solution, giving direct feedback from customers or end users.

q: In an interview, only the first question is fixed, and each later question follows from the previous answer. What type of interview is this?
explanation: In an unstructured interview the only question asked for certain is the first; later questions are based on the answers given. A structured interview works through a prepared list with the goal of asking every question.
ref: Business Analysis for Practitioners, How to Elicit Solution Information

links.label: Business Analysis for Practitioners, How to Elicit Solution Information

q: In a workshop, customers draw a boat and write on its anchors everything that holds the product back. Which collaborative game is this?
explanation: In speedboat, participants place the things they dislike about a product on anchors drawn on a boat, then discuss how much faster the boat would go if each were removed. It is a non-confrontational way to raise product issues.

q: A requirements workshop ended ten minutes ago. The analyst has four pages of notes that no stakeholder has reviewed yet. What is the status of those notes?
explanation: The output of Conduct Elicitation is the unconfirmed elicitation results. They become confirmed only when the product team reaches a common understanding and agrees they are accurate.

q: What is the purpose of Confirm Elicitation Results?
options: To obtain final sign-off on the solution
To check with stakeholders that what was captured is accurate and complete
explanation: Confirm Elicitation Results performs follow-up activities, reviewing the results with stakeholders for accuracy and completeness. Its key benefit is validating that the stakeholders and the results were understood.

q: What is a walkthrough?
options: A peer review in which the author leads the reviewers through the material
A tour of the customer's premises
A survey sent after a workshop
A test of the finished product carried out by end users before it is released
explanation: A walkthrough is a peer review in which the author of the materials walks the peer reviewers through the authored information. It can confirm that elicitation results are accurate or clarify discrepancies.

q: How does elicitation on an adaptive project differ from a predictive one?
options: It is done once, before development starts
It is frequent and in short cycles, eliciting just enough for the current and next one or two iterations
It is not done at all
It always produces a formal elicitation plan
explanation: In adaptive life cycles elicitation is frequent, aiming to elaborate just enough information for the current iteration or one to two iterations ahead. Predictive life cycles perform most elicitation and analysis up front.

q: A clinic's staff describe their booking process differently from the written procedure. What should the business analyst do?
options: Trust the written procedure, because it is the official one
Trust the staff, because they are the ones doing the work
Check a further source, for example by observing the process
Leave the difference for the developers to resolve during the build
explanation: Documents may be out of date and people may not describe their own work accurately. Observation can be used to cross-check other elicitation results against what actually happens.
